I have had a lot of success using a Weber and controling the temp with the vents. Basically close all but one on the bottom and then open up the top a little. Pile a bunch of charcoal on each side and heat up a smaller amount in a chimney. Then place some hot coals on your piles and use the vents to control temp. I have done a pork shoulder and ribs this way with a lot of success. I like to put a tin foil basin in the middle with apple cider or just water to keep the moisture up. Feel free to throw wood chips soaked in water on at any point to increase smoke flavor.

I'm partial to the offset smoker. The Oklahoma Joe's Longhorn and Highland models are solid. You can pick up a Longhorn from Walmart for under $300. I vouch for this smoker, and I'm a "buy it for life" type of guy. You can also use it for grilling, which is awesome.

So far I've done brisket, a whole turkey for Thanksgiving, 8 lbs of bacon, ribs, and just tonight I smoked some BBQ chicken for a few hours. Man, it's always good. The only downside about it is that sometimes the electrical connection comes loose and if you don't notice soon enough it can be a long night. I also use an iGrill with two probes to monitor smoker temp and meat temp. Takes about 10-15 minutes to get to 250° F. Alrighty I've got a dedicated smoker specifically

http://www.homedepot.com/p/Brinkmann-Heavy-Gauge-Off-Set-Smoker-and-Grill-855-6306-S/205501535?N=5yc1vZbx92

Here's what I've learned... while it's entirely possible to use the attached smoking unit on the bottom right to cook a meal it's only good for certain things, and it's unbelievably inefficient to use it as the only source of heat. Low cooked dried meats are best, although you can get a pork roast up if you've got about 8-9 hours and a ton of charcoal. It's a struggle to get the main unit hot, and to do a full smoke you'll need just about a full bag of charcoal and a lot of chips.

What I've started doing is putting a little coal in the upper unit right under the smoke stack (left side). This creates an updraft right where you need it and pulls the smoke a bit better from the other unit pulling the smoke up. It also takes less coal to keep the big part heated. At the bottom just use a tiny bit of coal and the metal wood chips unit (I usually fill it with water, and refill with soaked chips Jack Daniel's barrel chips being my go to). Then cook everything on the right side where the heat is most indirect. This is best for slow cooked burgers, pork, chicken, really anything that you'd normally grill.

Really knowing what I know now a large charcoal grill (just the upper unit of the linked) and cooking everything with the indirect heating method (putting all the coals in 1/4 to 1/3 of the grill and never placing anything directly above it) would work. All you need is a metal wood chips unit. You could make do with foil, but if you want to get fancy you could get a metal wood chips thing separate from the grill (it's basically a cast iron box with slits on the lid, fill it with water and wood chips and set it on the coals).

Hope that helps.

EDIT: IMO if you're doing this for BBQ you'll want to do the indirect heating method. If you're going to get into the 8 to 12 hour long smokes that produce dried meats and other smoked stuff get a dedicated one, but be aware of the time required and sheer amount of charcoal/wood you're going to consume.
